samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harold Paul Gross was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Harold Paul Gross. Mr. Gross served in the U.S. Army with the 24th Infantry Division. He served in the Pacific theater, and his highest rank was master sergeant. I'm Tom Swope. And this interview was recorded in Huntsburg, Ohio, on Paul's 84th birthday, July first, 2004.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you enlist in the army?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: I enlisted in the army on September 27th, 1940. They had passed the draft bill. They weren't drafting yet, and I was 20 years old and never started the draft at 21. In those days, you had to be 21 to be an adult. You had to sign for -- your parents had to sign for you, or you couldn't vote. So I was working in a grocery store for $9 a week, about between 55 and 60 hours a week, and happy to get the job. And a friend came in and said, "Let's go and join the army." We went and joined the army. We signed up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is there a reason why you chose the Army?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well yeah, I guess, because one of the friends wanted to go in the air corps. But I said, "No, I wanted to go into the army. I wanted to go into Signal Corps." I was interested in Signal Corps. So we went in and three of us went in but only two signed up, because one was not a high school graduate and the signal corps wanted high school graduates in those days. And so, he refused to go along, so two of us went. And we were sworn in down in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. And put on a train the next morning to New York City. Never been in a city before. People knew where we were going when we get off in Pennsylvania station and headed for New York -- what is it -- Grand Central Station -- on the subways and everything. Got on a train to -- can't think of the town now, but anyway, we went to Fort New York discharge and replacement depot in those days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't get to spend much time in New York City?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Oh no, not then. But we did have a -- I did have a one weekend pass later on. And we got to go to the very last day of the 1939 World's Fair. It extended for two years into 1940. Very last day of the World's Fair in New York. And got in for free, thank goodness, because we didn't have any money. Didn't even have money to buy lunch. We had to eat candy bars. [laughing]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about the World's Fair?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, it was pretty exciting, but I don't remember much about it, though. Except, it had a big electrical thing up there and gave the attendants that day. I think it was around a half a million or something. It was around the largest days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't go into the World of Tomorrow pavilion?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah. We did, because everything was free for us, because we were in uniform. We stayed in the soldiers and sailors club that night for 50 cents.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really? And that was in New York City?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: That was in New York City.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you go anywhere and have fun that night?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: No, but we walked down -- it was up -- we walked from Times Square right down to the Battery, which is I think about four miles with these new GI boots we had on that day. I had sore feet. Then, we walked up -- wherever the street that -- anyway, they said, "We're going to walk back." I said, "No way, I'm not going to walk that 4-mile back." We got back on the subway for a nickel, and went back on the subway.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were the people pretty nice to the guys in uniform in New York City?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yes. They were. I mean, they knew that we were -- [laughing] -- a bunch of hillbillies from the country. They told us where to go and all that kind of stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did you get along when you first got into the service as far as adjusting to guys from elsewhere in the country?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, as I said before, I think that -- that fellow that I enlisted with -- he got discharged about three weeks after we got there. I didn't even see him after the first day when we got -- next morning on a Saturday morning when we had our physical -- seemed for about three weeks, and they were discharging him. He had a hernia and he worked in the steel mill all the. But then I was there for a month or two then. Finally got a ship to Hawaii at a USAT, U.S. Army Transport Republic. Stopped at Atlanta picked up some more GIs down there. Went to the Panama Canal up the West Coast to San Francisco Bay. Spent a couple days there and then went on to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When was that? When was that crossing to Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: It was -- well, I got into Hawaii December 10th, 1940.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How was that crossing -- Pacific crossing?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, I was seasick the whole time. It wasn't a very good crossing anywhere. It was pretty horrible. But I don't want to go into the details of all that, because that was pretty horrible at the time. And I was -- actually in my five years in the service and in the Army, I spent total seven months on board ships. And the first three years, every time I got on one, I was deathly sick. This last two years, I got over it and never was sick once.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You think it's just because you just got used to it, or you were doing something different?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, I guess it was only about to last year, because we were headed into combat. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- other things on your mind maybe.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah, I guess so. Did never get sick after that at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, did you do your basic training then in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yes, we had six weeks of dismounted drill without arms. And we were restricted to an area. We couldn't go anywhere. We had restricted right to barracks there and I think we had six weeks. Then, we were assigned to our companies which I had enlisted for the 11th Signal Company -- Hawaiian Division it was in those days -- Hawaiian division. 11th Signal Company. Was there just -- since the war started on December 7th, 1941, and I got there 1940, I was just a year there when the war started.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's it like in Hawaii before the war started?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, it was pretty nice. I liked it. Of course, most of us were homesick. Even though I had met six other -- five other -- men from Pennsylvania. All gone to the same company -- 11th Signal Company. And we got to be friends -- friends throughout the time I was there. Nice and warm all the time. It was nice and breezy cool in the evenings. And you could smell those wonderful flowers all the time right through the air coming in. We had training and so forth. My training consisted of radio operator's training for -- I don't know how long -- couple, several months. But then, I was assigned to the photo identification unit -- ran the photo identification unit where people -- civilians that were coming on the base to be employed. And for that, and then a week -- just the week before December 7th, I was assigned to the Division Signal Office. And that's where I was when the war started.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you in the months proceeding that -- did you have any feeling that America was going into the war, that Pearl Harbor might be a target?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, of course, knowing they started the draft and they called in the National Guard and so forth. My attorney and I had a couple cousins were in the National Guard, Pennsylvania Division, and so forth. And 28th division. And of course, we're reading the papers. We knew that we were supporting Britain. We were sending stuff. People were starting to get jobs again, because it was manufacturing for Britain and so forth. You know, we read about the war and kept getting more serious. And actually, when the war started, we were on alert in the Hawaiian Islands, but we were on alert against internal rather than an attack from outside.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there any suspicion before the attack of the Japanese that were living there in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Not that I recall -- I mean, there was three companies in the barracks that we were in. The 11th Signal, the 11th Ordinance, and the 11th Quartermaster. And there was -- it was barbershop in the barracks and the barber was a Japanese man. Not to my knowledge. It was a pretty big Japanese population in the islands. And you'd see them, you know, on the streets in Honolulu and stuff like that when we got passes to go down there. And there were people working in the stores. Even on the base, there were Japanese people -- or Orientals. But no, I don't recall any specific.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you don't remember hearing any incidents of fighting spies or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, after the attack, there was all kinds of rumors then. In fact, the barber -- I don't know what happened to him, but he never came back. So I don't know, but -- I had a couple Japanese friends at the University of Hawaii. And one was just graduating. And he wanted to go to medical school at Harvard. And they let him go. But they met him -- he went by ship to San Francisco. They met him there and conducted all the way across the country to Harvard. Instead -- he went to school. He was Japanese. Became a doctor and I saw him years later in Honolulu. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any other stories from your training or anything before the attack. Any stories that come to mind?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: [laughing] Well, not really specifically in the training there. Because as I said it was -- but during the boot camp -- or what they call "boot camp" now. It wasn't called -- something different in those days. I got into trouble just once. [laughing] Sort of a story. As I said, we weren't allowed to leave the area. And just about -- I guess the weekend before we were going to get out and go to our companies, why, we found out that a couple fellows got permission on Sunday to go to church. Well, when they got permission to go to church, we says, "If they can go, we can go too." So we took off too and went to fee yaks and so forth. And then, next morning, had this all lined up. Some officer -- officer at that time -- and he gave us -- he was running us up and down. "And you ought to be ashamed of yourselves for doing this, you know." You ought to be ashamed of yourself. "That's right," he says, "bow your heads in shame." Well, I wasn't really ashamed of myself. I didn't agree with all I did, so I didn't bow my head. And of course, he saw me, and we had pith helmets in those days, because of the heat. And so, and the captain saw me, and he says, "See that man over there? Have him bow his head." So the corporal came over, and he told me to bow my head. I didn't say anything. I didn't bow my head. So he hit me somewhere went down my eye so it looked like I had my head bowed. So I did KP on Christmas Day. But it turned out to be pretty good; we got more to eat. More nice things on Christmas Day. But -- well we used to -- we looked forward to mail. And of course, the mail almost all -- it all came by ship which took some time. We didn't get it for weeks, for month -- from the East Coast. But once in awhile we'd get an airmail letter, which cost a lot in those days. And then, we looked forward to mail. And also, those that were homesick. I was homesick the whole first year. Until the war hit, and then, from then on, I was never homesick. But fellow used to say, "Well, they can say, I knew they were going to leave." You had a 3-year enlistment, but you only had to stay there two years. And after -- and I got close to going back home and say, "27 days and a bottle of milk" -- that was the breakfast the next day. And they would stay, and they'd yell out got when they got awake, sort of thing. "Only got 26 days" But I had a whole year yet, so I never got to that point.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Overall, did you get along with the officers?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yes. After the war started, I was a staff sergeant, but I was busted to a private. But that's a big story too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, let's hear that again.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: This is after the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Soon after it. Okay, go ahead and tell that, then we'll get back to.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Okay, I was a staff sergeant, chief clerk in the division signal office working for this colonel. And I got in an argument. One day I was only a corporal, so he made me a staff sergeant. Jumped sergeant completely and went through corporal staff sergeant. And then staff sergeant for awhile. And I disliked -- I didn't dislike him personally. I disliked what he did. I mean, he'd get me to get one of the colonels out in a field. And I had to go through a couple different switchboards and finally get colonel out in the field -- a full colonel -- and I'd turn around to give my lieutenant colonel the phone and he wouldn't be there. And so, I'd get chewed out. And a few things like that. But, I liked my job, actually. The job was a good job. Because the colonel before that was a very good colonel. But so, he gave the captain -- well, I wanted to get out of the company, so I applied for school down at the University of Hawaii, and I went to radar school for about six weeks. I got kicked out of there, because I knew that I could do the book work and the paperwork real well, but when it got to working on the equipment, the equipment didn't look the same as what the paperwork was. [laughing] So I got kicked out and I went back to the company. And I guess they didn't like that -- trying to get out of the company. So, the colonel gave the captain orders to bust me. And I was friends with the first sergeant, because he had been chief clerk in division signal office prior to me and I had worked for him. We were friends. He was from Idaho. He was a little bit younger than me. And I had made him first sergeant. So, he called me and said, "They're going to bust you, Gross. Just be on your toes." A couple weeks later, he called me -- captain, he kept me at detention for half hour in front of him. And then, he finally said "At ease." And he kept me there another half hour. And we discussed -- well, he discussed things and I listened. I gave him no argument whatever. It was "Yes, sir. No, sir." And he told me how smart I was. This that and the other thing. Trying to get me to say something. And I wouldn't say anything. So after an hour, he said, "You may leave, Private Gross." So I went upstairs, took my stripes off my shirt, which turned out to be a good thing again. Actually, it turned out to be a good thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right, let's go back to the weekend of the attack. What do you remember about that weekend?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah, it was on Saturday morning, weekend. On weekends, we -- unless you were on special duty for the weekend or anything -- why, you had free time from then on till Monday morning. And I was the mess hall. We were in the company; we had a real good mess hall -- good food, good cooks. And I gained about 20 pounds after I got to the service from eating well. And it closed -- the mess hall closed at 8 o'clock on weekends. And it was about seven minutes to eight, and I was debating whether I could get up and get dressed and get down and get something to eat when we heard these planes. And it kept getting louder and louder until -- we knew there was a lot of them, because it got so loud it shook you and you could vibrate in your chest. And by that time, we heard machine guns. And corporal said, "What are they clearing their guns for?" And so, he got up and went to the windows and pushed the screen open to look out. And by that time, they were in their dive. Terrible terrible explosion. And somebody yelled, "Plane's crashed." We thought it crashed. We went out on to -- the ones that were left went out on to the balcony. Third floor that we were on. Top floor of the barracks. We could see all these explosions and flame and debris flying up in the air, buildings flying apart and everything below us. And we says, "Hey, what's all this going on?" And then, all of a sudden, there was a Japanese plane went right by our barracks at eye level -- right at eye level. And the planes were slower then, especially these types of planes. And you could see the pilot sitting in there in the big red circle on the plane and everything. And we said, "Well, that's Japanese." So, we still were a little bit mystified what was going on. And then, so we got dressed and rushed downstairs to get our guns. The signal corps in those days was only -- we only -- the only weapons we had were .45 pistols. And they were in racks in the supply room. We didn't keep them in our barracks at that time. And we went down to get them and no officer had arrived yet. So the supply sergeant wouldn't give us our guns. He said, "I have to have an officer tell me to give you the guns." And the officers there, we got our guns; we got our ammunition. Then, we were told to report to our duty stations. And I reported to division signal office not knowing what to do. I'd only been there a week. Colonel -- it was in a little wooden building across one of the big infantry quadrangles. There was five quadrangles. It was third infantry quadrangle -- 19, 21st, 22nd infantry quadrant. Each hailed a regimen of troops. And oh -- I forgot to mention that we were no longer 11th Signal Company Volume Division. It was 24th Signal Company 24th Infantry Division, because on first of October 1941, they split the old Hawaiian division into two -- what they called "triangular divisions" with three regimens of infantry and so forth. And it was a different thing. So I reported to the Division Signal Office in this little wooden building. There was another friend of mine -- he was running the photo identification unit at that time. So he went with me. We weren't open photo identification. He went down to the Division Signal Office. There was nobody with me. We went in and pretty soon the colonel came in and he says, "Gross, answer the phone. Try to get a hold of me if you have to. I'm going to the telephone exchange" which was a mammoth exchange in those days. And his whole manual rather than mechanized things. And he says, "It's lit up like a Christmas tree over there. I'm going over to see if I can get it straightened out." And while we're sitting there waiting for the telephone to ring or whatever's going to happen, we could hear explosions in the distance and so forth. And all of a sudden, there was a big explosion right across the street from me, and there was couple infantry men were digging a gun emplacement there. Dug a big hole in front of them and knocked them right off a tree. And they sort of moved in slow motion, "What's going on?" You know? And as you said before, it was apparently a shell from the navy guns at Pearl, because there were no planes in the air over us at that time. So it couldn't have been a bomb. But I went later on and got a piece of shrapnel from it. And I still have it to this day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there much damage at Schofield Barracks?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: No, not to my knowledge. They strafed. They didn't drop any bombs on Schofield, they strafed very serious. And I never knew that there was anybody killed on unit, but I read an article from one of the -- just a year or two ago where he said he was driving a jeep and killed a man on the jeep sitting next to him. So, but I didn't know of any killed at that time. However, we did know sergeant and a lieutenant got on the roof at one of the quadrangles with Browning automatic rifles and shot down one of the planes. And I did see crashed planes in the days after we were driving around. We saw planes. Some of them crashed because they ran out of gasoline and so forth. But some of them were shot down. The pilots from Willard Field, they couldn't get any planes in the air because there was damage on the runways. In fact, they practically destroyed all the planes. Hit six of the nine big hangers over there. And 50 years later, they were still there. They managed to get their planes down in the little airstrip down on the north shore. And they got their cars and went rushing down there and called ahead to heather to have their guns ammunition put in them and all this kind of stuff. They did shoot down three or four planes. Well, then they blacked out the barracks and put stuff in the windows so we have anything. Dug slit trenches with the machinery outside the barracks and everything. We didn't know whether the Japanese were going to land troops or not. But at that time, there were all kinds of rumors that they had landed troops and paratroopers and so forth. But it all turned out to be false. Just rumors as they go flying around. But that's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you probably have some to show -- I was going to ask what the rest of that day was like? Nerve wracking?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah, after that shell hit across the street, I don't remember much about the day after that. Except I talked to a couple guys that went to -- went down to the Wheeler Field right next door to us to help out down there picking up bodies. And I guess they didn't like it and they came back. And they did hit. I think it was somewhere between two and three hundred. Most of them were killed in the big main -- they had a main big mess hall there that fed everybody which was different. We ate in each barracks. And they hit the mess hall, and that's where a lot of them were killed. And they dug slit trenches behind our training area and laid them into boxes and put them in and covered them up. I think later on years later I think they -- but they buried most of them behind our training there in the barracks. And then, they set up a -- they started bringing in planes -- bringing in P-40s while the -- they made an airstrip out of the golf course which was -- from our windows, we could see one whole area of the golf course. And that's where these P-40s landed. And it was slightly sort of uphill. And I come in here. It was pretty hard. They bounce 50 feet. [laughing] We saw two or three of them crash because they hit too hard and down would go their landing gear on one side or something like that. And they over into the trees. But they had planes everywhere. And then P-40s.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Can you see Pearl Harbor from Schofield Barracks?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: No, you couldn't see Pearl Harbor, but we could see the smoke and stuff. It's about -- I don't know -- around probably ten miles. It's of course at sea level and Schofield Barracks is up in the middle in the central part of the island. And it slopes down on both ways from north shore to south shore from there. So you could see and hear smoke and explosions and stuff. But that's -- but Schofield, we look right together and that's where.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you getting any kind of reports from what was happening down at the harbor?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, just accepted -- but about five days later, I drove a truck down to -- first time I ever drove a truck -- I drove a truck down to Honolulu. Went past Pearl Harbor and all we could see is just ships. Couple of them tops of the ships hanging out of the water, sticking out of the water and everything. But we did then get word every day from the newspapers that the Oklahoma had turned turtle with a lot of men were inside of her. They couldn't use torches, because there was air in there. So they use chippers to chip steel. They got men out of there for up to -- I think -- something like a week or eight days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were thinking when you got a look in the harbor?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah, I thought it was a little different than what was coming over the radio. Radio says they sunk one ship and damaged -- boy, it looked a lot worse than that. Well, we didn't want it to -- but thank goodness, they didn't hit any carriers, because the carriers were out. The carriers were out that weekend. So they didn't get any of the carriers. They got the battleships was what they were after. And they got the battleships. But it would probably have been better off for them and worse off for us if they had hit all the oil storage tanks and stuff like that which they didn't. It was easy to replace the ships than it was to replace some of the other stuff, I think.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what happened next for you then in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, I stayed there for another year and a half till May of '43.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: We were talking about what you did in Hawaii after this episode.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah, well again, I was in the Division Signal office when the chief clerk -- after the war, when they did this reorganization to different type of infantry divisions and the war came along they upped the grades everywhere. And the division signal officer became a tech sergeant, but he was only a sergeant at that time. And so, they -- our regular first sergeant was transferred back to the states to form new companies and so forth. So they made him first sergeant and I became chief clerk in the division signal office as a corporal which called for a tech sergeant which was a long way off. And when everybody started getting promotions in the company, I got sort of upset. And that's when I had a little discussion with the colonel. And I said about a week later I was a staff sergeant. I skipped buck sergeant completely and went from corporal to staff sergeant. And then, of course, I got busted to a private. And then, in May of '43, all of a sudden, I was only a -- what was I? A T-5, which was Technician Fifth Grade. All of a sudden, it was noticed on the bulletin board that Paul in 33 name would be transferred to grade and so forth. And they showed the grades, and I went from a T-5 to a Tech Sergeant. I skipped all the grades in between. So I never was a Buck Sergeant. And I would be transferred to mainland to form a new outfit for divisions that they were forming. And so, then we -- boy, we were happy. [laughing] And we got back to Camp San Luis Obispo, California. And we were there only a short time when we got word that our officer -- there was one officer that transferred with us -- we got word that he was a captain. We got word that they weren't forming anymore divisions. They decided we had enough divisions and so forth. They didn't know what to do with us. And so, we sat there for -- let's see, we were back there in Maine -- we were back June, July, August -- a few months. Did a little training there. Part of the 96th Division was there. And they moved them out to get rid over seas. And so, they grabbed me because I could type. They grabbed me to the teletype machines. I never operated a teletype. I managed to get through that. All of a sudden, in September, they transferred us up to Port Or California. We were going to form a new company, but we didn't know what kind. That's when we formed a 94 Joint Assault Signal Company. And we had -- they kept bringing in men from other organizations. Usually from signal organizations or headquarters organizations and so forth. Till we had about 400 men and around 45 officers. It was a major perk. Our captain didn't become the commander, because they put a major in charge. And they had a major for a company commander. Had a number of captains and a whole lot of lieutenants. Ten master sergeants. And I then was promoted to a master sergeant. So, and that's what I was the rest of the war. So we took training there. We took -- after we got the company formed. And there was a sort of funny one. When we got new people, we tried to made them into three or four of us master sergeants were assigned to give them a bit of dismounted drill without arms. Which I had done. I never done this kind of thing with a rifle. Because we'd never been -- when we were finally armored with rifles, we didn't have any training on them, just fired them. And so, I had a platoon. And I watched this other master sergeant who had been in the infantry awhile. When he yelled something then I yelled it too. So I knew what to do till I got on to it. And then, we took some bayonet training and stuff like that. And some, of course, you're always going to gas training. We took a bunch of training there. And then, we started our amphibious training in the bay there -- what's the town?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Monterey or?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah, Monterey Bay. We were going to start our amphibious training there. Well, after about one day, we decided that was not enough -- the conditions weren't good for training and that kind of thing. So they moved the whole company down to Kent Pennell Marine Base to try our amphibious training with the marines. And first sergeant -- I'll tell this story I didn't tell before. The first sergeant -- about three days before the company was to leave, he calls me and he says, "Hey, Gross, you're first sergeant to them for the next few days. I'm going down to Camp Pendleton." Ahead of time and he says, "You're in charge." Well, I'd never been first sergeant in a big outfit like that. So, but -- so, the day came to leave. They brought us -- we brought a train into the area there and we loaded up the train. But in the meantime, I had to clear the base. And I never in my life realized how much there was to clearing a base with a company like that. And I had a guy drive me in a jeep and we were all over the base signing papers, signing papers. We were supposed to leave by three o'clock. By three o'clock, I was still signing papers. We got back, and here was a train smoking there and everything, just waiting on me to get on that train. We get on that train and then after awhile they come up to me -- the conductors on the train come up to me and they said, "Sign these papers." And they had 412 men. And I said, "No, not 412. I only got 405 here. You've got seven too many." Well, no, I'm not going to sign for more than what's on here. I know the government's going to pay for these people. I says, "We don't have 412 men." Boy, they were upset. So what they had to do, we had officers on board. So they got two of our officers and they started in the train and we counted the whole train. I was correct. The conductors weren't very happy, but we signed the papers with the -- and then, we got down to the yards in Los Angeles which is north of Camp Pendleton, and we were parked there awhile. And here another train pulled up alongside and it was -- I had never seen them before -- it was Mexican seaman. And we couldn't talk to them, because they were speaking Spanish. Then, we went down to Camp Pendleton. We took about six weeks of amphibious training down there which turned out to be -- it was pretty rough. We made landing. They brought other companies in there for training there and everything. And I was an observer as a master sergeant and a couple others were made observers on landings and some of the other companies. And that was when I got -- they said, "There's Colonel James Roosevelt." And he was standing over there. And I thought, "Boy, he's a big guy." So I walked over behind him. I never did shake hands or salute him or anything. He was standing watching this thing. So I walked up -- he was a big man Colonel James Roosevelt. Never did say anything to him. But and then we made a landing ourselves on San Clemente Island. They were shelling ahead of us with one destroyer out there shelling the place. And they had Bangalore torpedoes on there. And there was infantry too, not just our company. There was infantry battalion making a landing. Couple guys got injured -- not our men, but infantry men got injured when the Bangalore torpedoes exploded after they got on the beach rather than before they got on the beach. And then when I got to shore, we were running up to one of the canyons there and I passed this lieutenant -- he was going around in a circle. Just a nice big circle. Just kept going around in a circle. And I looked at him. The shell had hit pretty close to him. So that he was really didn't know what he was doing. And then, he came and got him and took him away. But then, that was it for that landing. It was -- there was no people living on San Clemente. Just some animals. I'll tell you, the landings. We made a landing on a strand there in San Diego. Just practice landings. Off of a LCI, Landing Craft Infantry. And you had ladders down each side of the bow. And I was first officer. I thought it wasn't close enough, but I went up to my neck in [chuckling] But you had your rifle over your hands and everything. And we've been on landings there where our lieutenant saved a couple guys. They made -- they broached the boat. And when you broach them like that, if a wave hits, they roll over. And I almost caught a couple of them under because it threw them off and everything. And he managed to save them and everything. So we had no one injured in our company or nothing like that. And then, we -- we were all split up into various teams with the infantry. We'd be assigned to infantry battalions and so forth each team. We had signal teams and artillery teams and naval teams and direct naval fire and direct air strikes and direct artillery fire. And we finally got all together up at Camp Beale, California to go overseas, and we went to Hawaii on a ship -- just our company on a ship a little smaller ship. It's a nice little ship. And, but we were by ourselves. We weren't escorted. It was a little later. And we weren't escorted though. And went to Hawaii, spent about a month there, getting all of our equipment in shape and getting the new equipment that we were waiting for coming from the manufacturers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay, continue.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before I split, you should describe how early was the joint assault company supposed to go in on the landings?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: We were trained to go in with the third and fifth waves of infantry. It never turned out that we -- only once, I think -- some of our men went on the third or fifth wave. Because of the way the situation -- that's the way you were trained to do it that way, but situation changes as you. And as I think I mentioned before, at least ten signal teams. One was just an extra team in case anything -- we lost a team or anything like that. The other nine teams were each assigned to an infantry battalion. I was assigned -- our lieutenant -- they drew straws as to which battalion would you get assigned to. We didn't draw the straws -- you were assigned battalions. When they made the landings, at that time, the way it was set up, if you had a division with three regimens of infantry and three battalions in each regimen, there would be two regimens on the initial landings with one regimen in reserve to throw in where they needed. And of the six battalions that would be on those two regimens going in originally, it would be only four in the actual first assault waves. And then, each regimen had one battalion ready to throw in where it was needed. So in the original, out of nine battalions of infantry, you only had four hitting the beach on the first waves of troops. And so, that's why we only had a few men actually went in on the third and fifth waves because of that. The battalions that we were with -- that I was with -- my team and my officer was with -- were always drew in the reserves. So we didn't go ashore the morning the second day usually. Or Lusan, went the couple about four hours because we didn't have any really resistance there. But there was four divisions abreast. We landed four divisions. And so, the whole task force was about a hundred thousand men with all kinds of ships to support us and everything. About 600 ships. Actually, I read it was 800, but I always thought it was 600 actually.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And what landing was that?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: All three landings -- Leyte, Lusan, and Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you in Hawaii before you went to the Philippine Islands?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: About a month. Actually we didn't take off to go to the Philippines when we were on ship. We loaded on board these APAs -- that's troop carriers -- ships -- able to handle about battalion usually or less of the men. They were all loaded on the decks with just big stacks of plywood and we wondered what the plywood was. After we sailed, we found out they were going to build little scowls to put our equipment on. Because we said we were going to yap. And the Japanese had brought up big counsel defense guns from Singapore and they knew where they were located and they knew where the machine gun nests were -- at least some among the shore. So there was a reef about a half mile offshore. And they couldn't get the landing crafts over that. So, they were going to put us out there, and we were going to wade ashore and half mile with these -- pushing these little things with our equipment in them. And we says, "Oh, no, we don't want to do that." Well, after about three or four days, they took all intelligence reports and everything away from us and says, "Forget it." So we sailed and sailed, and we went to the Manus Island in Admiral Islands. It's about 2 degrees south of the equator. The navy was building a big base there. It was a big harbor in between the islands there. And we stayed there for -- I don't know the actual days. We were on board ship that time for 37 days. So I don't know just how long we stayed there. But, we stayed there. And all of a sudden we took off and there was about 600 ships and 25 escort carriers with just a few planes each and so forth. But then we were supported by a whole fleet of -- I don't know what it was hol gee I don't know who the navy guy was at the time. But we sailed intelligence reports and everything about Leyte. Well, we didn't know where Leyte was, but they told us it was in the Philippine Islands. They told us what it's going to be like when we hit there and everything like that. And we knew what it was like. So we went there and hit there. The ship I was on, they -- of course, a lot of these areas were mined and everything. They took in mine -- what they call mine-destroyer ships or something. They'd go in ahead of time and look for mines and everything. But ship I was on lost its port paravane -- the paravanes were out on each side. If they hooked onto a mine cable, it would flip the cable up the nine up and they could shoot them. We lost our port paravane. But, nothing happened. And we went in and we made landing there on the 20th of October. I was on board the ship -- I don't remember the name of it anymore -- but, we were on board a ship that they had a bunch of doctors on they were going to use to bring casualties on board. So I didn't go in the next day and I saw them bring in the casualties. And that was the first. I mean, these are wounded casualties -- not dead ones. Saw some couple -- we weren't supposed to be, but we got to see a couple of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did that affect you when you saw that?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: We were all sort of scared. [chuckling] Sort of scared. It's sort of like going to the dentist. I never really got scared till I got in the dentist chair. That was the way it was there. I didn't really get scared till we were actually there. But we were under air attack. And that night -- the first night -- boy, our navy laid down these smoke screens and the Japanese planes were coming in everywhere. I saw as many as three Japanese planes in the air at one time -- balls of fire that got hit. I still have a couple color slides. We weren't supposed to have cameras, but I took a camera with me. And I got a few pictures. Boy, it was like they plowed up the place. And there's the big coconut palms were all stripped. I mean, just palms hanging down everywhere. And there were some Filipinos coming by trying to get out of the way of the soldiers and everything. I got a few pictures there. And then, I don't remember -- I can -- there's lots of things I remember, but I don't remember specifically the order or anything anymore, because used to know the names of the towns we were at. We landed near San Miguel or something, I forget. I do remember the name of the hill that overlooked the beach. It was Catman Hill. And that's where got wounded on the beach. They shelled the beach with mortars for awhile before they knocked him out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what else do you remember about that campaign even if you don't remember the names, places?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, we sent main team communications for about -- once the troops were far enough inland far enough that the navy guns wouldn't reach, why they took out those teams. I was in the signal team, but they took out those team. But we still had some men in the forward OPs directing air strikes. We had air teams too. And they direct the air strikes. And if they call -- if the infantry called for them. And we had -- when we called for artillery, if I recall correctly, when we call for artillery fire, they'd usually fire one round of what they call "Willy Peter White Phosphorous" which would mark the area. And if that was it, why the infantry would say, "Let her go." See? So. And I remember one of the guys -- he forgot to repeat, when they said "I am -- I repeat." And they fired the whole round of white phosphorous through his head. [laughing] So there was few things that -- but there was a lot -- you know, there's a lot of friendly fire. When the shells and everything start flying, boy, everybody gets excited, and they start firing. Thank goodness, I never had anybody firing at me, and I didn't have to fire my rifle. But we were under attacks coming in and things like that. We were told by our officers -- and I don't know how true it was -- that there was 12 men accidentally the first day we were ashore. But it's possible -- when the shells start pluming, boy, they just. I made a run-in dash into a -- dove head first into a slit trench. Everything was cut loose and there was Japanese plane coming right -- we were right on the beach. I was, oh, about -- maybe 50 yards from the water. And about 150 peter. So I dove into this trench. And boy, it was just everywhere -- everything flying and everything. I stuck my head up to see what was going on, and here was this plane -- looked like it was coming right at me. He was right at water-level. I mean, he was just down -- and we knew he was going to hit. But they did hit him, and he crashed right on the beach here. And exploded and killed a couple of guys there on the gun position. But in the planes -- thank goodness, just a little to my left -- the planes went back to my left. And felt the heat off of them of course, and everything, but that was the end. That was sort of scary [chuckling] You don't have any control -- that's the thing. It's like I never did like flying after the war. But we only stayed there about -- I don't know -- three weeks, one month. And they loaded us on an OST. And there were a number of OSTs lined up on the beach down from us a ways about a half mile from us on the beach. And we had to transport all of our equipment everything to the OST and load up all the weapons -- everything -- motor vehicles and everything onto is this OST. We loaded one OST. I was on the shore end of it where we were putting -- we had men on the OST positioning the vehicles and so forth. And Japanese planes come in, attacked, and our men were carrying -- our men on the ship were carrying ammunition for the guns for the navy because they were really using it up. They were coming -- and one kamikaze was coming right at the fantail of the ship where our men were on. And the navy was firing the guns and they hit the guy and swerved and hit the guy next and exploded on the fantail of the gun. So, we always figured we were the most lucky organization in the whole darn army. Because number of killed and wounded we had was ridiculous compared to -- and then, so then we missed the convoy that left that night. We missed it, because we didn't get fully loaded. We were too busy carrying ammo and so forth. The two ships that got hit and ours that didn't get out. And so, we waited a day or two there, and we took off ourselves. And we went unescorted to -- well, we stopped in New Guinea first and then went to New Britain. Unescorted -- but when we got into New Guinea, some of our officers went ashore and the convoy that we missed had been under air attack by Japanese planes in the night. And when our ship didn't get there with them, they thought we got sunk. And they were preparing -- the navy was preparing teletypes to -- with the names that they had. But they didn't send them because our men got ashore and said, "Oh, we're here." Then, we went on to New Britain, spent about -- I don't know -- three weeks there in the jungles out on the beach there equipping - re-equipping and cleaning up our equipment and all this kind of stuff. And by the way, it was sixth army on Leyte. I don't remember which army it was on Lusan, but anyway, we got back on a troop transport, went to the Manus Island in the airbornes again and waited and there came all these ships and we went to Lusan. We landed there what? I don't remember -- it was the 7th -- 7th of January -- ninth, I think. I don't remember 7th or ninth. I believe 7th. 7th of January. And they shelled that place -- boy, four divisions again made the landings there. And we were with the 96th division on Leyte. Now we were assigned to the 40th division on Lusan. But we didn't have any opposition at all. The Japanese stopped and we shelled past -- knew we were going to land somewhere near Batan somewhere where fighting had been before. And they pulled all their troops out that night and everything. So we didn't have much opposition there. So, we didn't have much of a job to do. But we stayed there -- again, for maybe two weeks or a month. And they put us on a troop transport again. This time an A P A. I hated that, because we had to load on those ships with all our equipment hanging on us -- guns, ammunition, pack, and climb those nets. And I didn't have very strong arms. I had strong legs, but not arms. Of course, I got the bow net. And the bow net is the highest and the one that slopes back underneath. Almost didn't make it to the top of that thing that time. But, we had a lot of training on what to do if we fell. If you fell between them and the ship or something, you had it. But we had training on what we should try to do. Anyway, I made it up to the top -- and we made it -- because some guy helped me thank goodness [chuckling]. And then, we went back down to Leyte -- fighting was still going over on the west side of Leyte around Ormoc -- city of Ormoc. And 24th Division was fighting over there. Oh, I forgot to say that, when we were on Leyte the first time -- our old op -- we were 96th Division. and the 24th division was on our right flank. They were on our -- half of our -- 14th -- corps. I don't remember if it was 14th or I corps, which one it was now anymore. But we managed -- we didn't have anything to do after the fighting. We got permission to go see if we could find our old outfit. We did find it after -- boy, wrote on the back of a two-and-a-half ton carrying drums of gasoline. We road on the gasoline trunks. And then, we got a jeep ride. And we went to an area where the 24th had just had a big battle with the Japanese and driven them out -- well, driven them out, there was about hundreds of them laying dead all along the way. It was terrible. The smell was awful -- you couldn't stand it. We finally found our old outfit. Well, at least the division signal office we found. We didn't get the other guys. Met the lieutenant who now was a major in division signal officer. And the man that had assigned us all to this. He was the one that came up the list assigned us to go back to the States originally to form this new outfit. So, [chuckling] Name is Dabrico [sp]. Lieutenant Dabrico. Very good officer -- everybody liked him. Then, when we got back to Leyte the second time, we stayed there about a month. Let's see -- October, January, February, March, April. We probably stayed there a month or more and set up tents and mess hall and everything there. And got our equipment. And that's where we got our first packages from home -- Christmas packages and everything. This was in February, late February, and got our Christmas packages. And they had dumped them on the beach from the ship and everything. And oh my, about 99 or 10 or more were absolutely. And mail, we got some mail. And I think we got it -- while we were there, we got a partial payment. That's the first. We were there about six months. And already we got a partial payment. I think 20 dollars or something like that. But there was nowhere to spend it. [laughing] So we saved our money. And then, we got back on a troop transport again, and we headed for Okinawa. And this time, we were 10th Army. 96th Division was back, and we were with the 96th Division. And that was a good fighting outfit. They lost a lot of men on Okinawa. And went to Okinawa. And I watched all the showing -- the showing bombardment that night was something you never forget. You couldn't see the island. It was just explosions and dirt and dust and smoke. You couldn't see anything except -- and I didn't go ashore the morning the second day again there. Going to the beach -- I was on the beach there. I was there long enough on the beach that we saw replacements coming in for the wounded and everything. Navy ship was one of those replacements. Brother-in-law didn't know him in those days. But he was probably one of those replacements. Came in for the 77th Division. But the fighting went on, the landings four divisions that landed -- I think was three army and one marine division landed from the original landings. And the island there is sort of -- divided into small one-fourth or so island in the south and the north is about three quarters of it. But there's nothing up there but farms and stuff like that. The city of Naha was in the southern part and so forth. And that's where most all the Japanese troops were. So they landed, went across the island, about two miles wide at that point or three miles wide. First day, turned south, 19 days later they hadn't gotten anywhere. Bombardment on the 19th or 20th day was -- you couldn't -- it was just saw explosions, bombs, hills, everything. And then as chick said in his report that it was one hill right after another -- or ridge, they were ridges ran all across the island in places. The Japanese were dug in from one side to the other. They had tunnels that went all the way to the ridge and had holes underground. And they had inflating fires where the ridges wouldn't form pockets. They had inflating fire. It was terrible for the troops. Chick knows very well. And we could -- we were then moved up bivouacked next to the airstrip there. Ka dean airfield. And some of our men were helping communications and so forth with the airfield. And darn it was a big Japanese -- later there was a railroad gun that they had on tracks and it was in a big cave. And when they'd throw it out. They'd shoot one or two or three rounds every night. Big gun boy, and it hit that. First time it ever happened, we were on our jungle hammocks strung between little pine trees and so forth. And all of a sudden we heard this swoosh and boom and boy it shook the trees. And we were rocking around and everything. We zipped out of those things in a hurry. And found some caves along the side of the hill and got in there. They fired that thing every night for about a month. And they couldn't knock that thing out. Reason was, because they fired some rounds, run it back in, next day, they'd shell that area. And then, they'd dig it out the next day, lay some track down. Next night, fire couple rounds, put it back in again. But the air corps was really upset, because it destroyed some of their planes and it kept their pilots up at night. And they were upset with it. Every day, I said we got it today. And every day, they didn't get it. Finally, it was taken by the marines -- took the gun. Watch the fire and about 50 seconds later we could hear the shell coming and everything. So, it was a big one, so it did a lot of damage on the airstrip there couple times. But -- and then, sometime later, I got to go up towards the front, head of the -- I don't know why -- artillery. You know you can see an artillery shell if you're behind it and fired. You can see the thing going. And we were head of the artillery. But we went up to Naha. And Naha was flat. It was a city of about 75,000. They even had trolley cars and stuff, but it was flat. And the only building I found sufficiently large that I could take a picture of where we were was at been a Christian church. And it was a one wall standing. It looked like cement blocks stuff. One wall standing and the cross was still on top. And I got a picture of that too. And I have friends now, we have a friend that lives here in Ohio, after the war, G I -- he wasn't in World War II. He married a gal from Okinawa. And they're friends now. Her name is Ta key. So we stayed there the whole time. And the whole three months up to the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job specifically at Okinawa when you were?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, in Okinawa, because of the -- these organizations joined sal signal companies were a new idea for them to -- for the central communications on the beaches. Because they were having trouble with that. But, you weren't -- I don't know how many -- I only knew of four in the army. And we had the most combat time and the least casualties. That's why we say we're so lucky and everything. But what was the question?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I just asked what your job was.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Oh yeah, well, after Leyte -- I have some of the -- in our company history, which one of our lieutenants actually wrote a few years ago, put together, we have some of the declassified secret things that were sent in how our company operated. And how successful we were and everything. And they found out that having a team with teachers of battalions didn't work too well. So they made only -- instead of having nine teams, we had three teams, one larger team with each regimen. From then on, it was red men. So we only had three of the master sergeant. I don't know what happened to the some of the other ones. But this captain that originally helped set up the company; he said he asked for me to be supply sergeant, because our supply sergeant was back in Hawaii. And actually wasn't a sergeant then, he was warrant officer. But he asked me to be supply sergeant. And he asked for me. And he said, "Do you mind?" And I said, "No, I don't mind one bit." And he happened to be an officer that nobody in the company -- nobody, liked. It's unfortunate. But in my time there in the supply sergeant there on Okinawa, I got to know the man. He was a Texas A&M graduate. I got to know him a little bit. And you know, I got to like the guy. Felt sorry for him, because he tried his best. He wanted the men to like him. And everything he did was wrong -- every damn thing he did was wrong. And he poured his heart out to me because he could talk to me and everything. And I felt sorry for the man. When we had our reunions, the first reunions, I guess he was gone already. I never got in touch with him. I worked for him, because he treated me fine. It was just, he couldn't do anything right. So I was supply sergeant on Okinawa. And we set up tents and VX -- little VX where we had some -- few things, candy bars and some stuff like that. One of the other stars -- one of the master sergeant. And one night, there was big hill and our tents were on the bottom of the hill. There was a little bit of a stream ran down to that little bit of a valley. And there was a little airstrip for light planes, for sputter planes they were using down from us a ways. We couldn't see them, but we could hear them once in awhile. And they had trip wires around the whole area, because Japanese would sneak in and hit one of those trip wires. Why, it'd set off a flare, and they'd get at them. Well, one night, I had already gone to the bed, and we had folding cots and everything in these 12-man tents. And fighting was still going on in front of them, but we were back in rear areas. And all of a sudden, I heard somebody swearing and splashing around and everything. I got out and I went to get out of bed out of my bunk and there he was. The water was right up to the pack and everything. They were enlarging that little airstrip in the day or something and the bulldozers had pushed dirt over this little stream and it dammed it up and it came up into our house got all of our equipment wet and our clothes and everything else. And then, one night, one of our men told a Japanese infiltrating, he didn't -- it really bothered him to have killed a person. That was the first any time. Then, we captured one too. One of our guys -- one of the most quiet guys in the company -- they found out he spoke Japanese. And they had him question him. Found out he spoke something like eight languages. We never heard him speak anything, because he was so quiet and everything. But, he spoke about eight languages. And one of them being Japanese. But then, they turn him over to intelligence people afterwards. So we stayed there. Then, right up till the end of the fighting. But that time the war had ended in Europe, and they were already getting outfits being shipped to the Pacific to replace -- getting ready for the big operation. And our first sergeant -- motor sergeant -- man we pulled out flew back to the states -- flew him back to the states -- I guess he got discharged, because they had so many points. And I had the next amount of points myself and a couple of other fellows. And we thought, "When are we going to get pulled out? When are we going to get pulled out?" And finally, after a couple weeks, they said, "Oh, you're going to get pulled out now, but you're going to set up a camp for all the rest of the guys and things." So we went up to the hill there and set up a camp made some showers out of 55 gallon drums and stuff like there. Set up some tents. I still there. All of a sudden they said, "Okay, we got a ship for you." And they put us on a ship and found out it was going to take Japanese prisoners back to the states. Never saw any prisoners except on -- just once before on Lusan -- but, we were bivouacked. The army had set up a big field hospital just close to us -- real close to us there -- had nurses and everything, but they never put anybody in it. Then, they turned that over to -- they had Okinawa nurses and stuff, but they didn't use our nurses or anything. And I managed to get over there and get us through those wards and see those guys -- those wounded Japanese. So we were going to take Japanese back to the States. And typhoon came along, so they put out to sea for a day or two to ride out the typhoon rather than being caught in the bay there. And so, they got back in and they says, "Change our mind." So somebody knew something then -- weren't going to take these things back. So we got on this -- so the ship took off and we're going along for a couple of days and all of a sudden we put in the Ulithian -- the western Carolines -- and the captain called us in and said, "I got orders to go to the Philippines to pick up troops." We says, "Is this closer to the States than the Philippines?" He says, "Yeah." We says, "We'll get off here." [laughing] So, we got off in Ulithian, it was a beautiful place. I mean, you had -- before the war, they had a coaling station there for ships and so forth. But it was white sand and palm trees. And it was pretty. It was nothing higher than about five feet off the bar. So, we spent a few weeks there. They gave us -- we got a -- since the navy had a V X and everything there. Why, we got a partial payment. I think we got 20 dollars, so we could buy a few things. I don't know how many of us there were, but ship came along and it was an old president liner that had been junked back in the 30s, and they took it out of the junk yard and put it back in service. And it was loaded with other troops and they took us on board. I don't know, it must have been a thousand men on it. It was terrible. It was terrible. We only got fed two meals a day, and the food was rotten when we got it -- the meat and everything. Guys were complaining. That's when I got into trouble again -- [laughing]. Well, I had -- I was in charge of a hundred men, and I got to know -- none that were in our company, but I got to know a couple of them. I can even remember what a couple of them looked like. One staff sergeant. And there are some darn good men in those companies, I'll tell you. But they kept complaining to me, "Gross, we're not getting fed enough." When an officer -- they had this captain -- army captain in charge of the troops on the ships and everything. He had a couple lieutenants. And he sent a lieutenant down there. And while he was standing there, they put more food on the tray. When he'd leave, they'd cut it down. And the men would complain about this. And half of what they got weren't fit to eat anyway. They kept complaining to me, "Why don't you do something?" I said, "What am I going to do?" So I talked to a couple people in the management. I finally got a master sergeant that I didn't know, but he agreed to go with me, and we got permission to go see the captain on board in charge of troops. And so, we also got in touch with the ship's chaplain. And he said, "Yeah" he'd go in with us. Well, we went in, and it turned out I did all the talking. The chaplain and the master sergeant had nothing to say. So, I told the captain what to -- oh, by the way, when we walked in, he had a sink in the corner of his thing, and there was a chunk of ice in the sink, and he had a little table there with bowl on it with some fresh fruit in it, apples and so forth. And so, he was getting fed anyway. So I told him what was happening. I says, "Your man stands down there. Your lieutenant stands down there, and they put some food in when he leaves, but when he turns around, it gets cut down. At the end, what we got." And boy, he lit into me, and he called me a liar and everything else. Well, I kept my cool, except that I said, "Well, I've been in this army five years and I know a little bit about it. I know what's going on." I says, "Some guys are getting some money in your pockets here," meaning him, but I didn't say it. [chuckling] So anyway, I said "I request permission to go show the first report we put into it that has an I G and I'm going to see the I G." Well, the first report we put into was Honolulu. Nobody was allowed ashore. But I took up a collection, and I got permission to go ashore to get jackets from my group of a hundred men. I didn't care about all the rest of them because I didn't have anything to do. I got permission to go ashore to get I Gs. I don't think I ever got the jackets -- I don't remember -- but I took up a collection of the money we had and I went to the commissary or V X or something on the -- and all the money I had, I bought candy bars and cans of juice and stuff like that. And I hauled those back on board ship for my hundred men. And so, we had something the last -- we were about another seven days to the states. And so, they were happy. At least my group of men were happy and everything. But [chuckling] But I never did go to the I G or anything. I was on my way home. Then, we got into -- gee whiz -- we got into San Francisco now. Remember, we'd been on a ship that had put in on Ulithian, then we got on this ship that only go about seven knots downhill with the tail wind on it. And so, when we got into San Francisco, here's some of the men from our company that we had left in Okinawa and they had gone from Okinawa to Leyte and got disbanded. The company was already -- what we call it -- disbanded or something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Decommissioned?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Yeah, decommissioned. And here are some of our men standing on the dock there when we pulled in and everything. Doggoned it. They got back to the states before I did. But anyway, I don't know what some base went to around San Francisco there. And about three days later, they flew me across country to Fort Dix, New Jersey on an old C-47. Took us 24 hours to fly across country. Landed about three places to refuel and everything and got into Fort Dix. Since I had listed in the third corps area, they discharged me from Fort Dix New Jersey. And they were discharging groups of a hundred. 24 hours a day, hundred going to. That's the first I saw -- they were a time they were prisoners of war, but they were no longer prisoners of war, but they were serving food in the mess hall and stuff like that. And then, he called another master sergeant myself into another room. We were both regular army. Tried to talk us into staying. Neither one stayed, because I told him I wanted to go to college, which I did. I had five years of college eligibility and I went to five -- I graduated from Baltimore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back home after?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Well, my mother had -- my dad during the war when I was home once when we came back to the states, I had leave to go back to Pennsylvania, of course, it took five days by train, because the train had to stop for troop trains and everything like that. So I had a few days back home. And I talked to him. And they were trying to hire people for Kaiser shipyards out in the west coast Oregon and Washington up there. Shipyards everywhere were trying to hire people, because there were so few people yet, you know, available. So I talked to him, and he applied and he got accepted. So when I went back to California, we road by train together to Chicago. Then, he got on train that went up to Washington and everything. He worked up there for awhile, but my dad was -- I always said he couldn't adapt to the modern living. And he just couldn't stand being away from Pennsylvania and everything. And I don't know how he ever got back to Pennsylvania. He quit work and eventually got back to Pennsylvania. But anyway, my mother in the meantime, as I said before, when I enlisted in the army, my father, my mother, and two younger sisters and myself were living in one room -- no electricity, no running water. So, it wasn't hard for me to enlist. And I helped my mother by sending her money and this kind of stuff. But, she had moved to Berea, Ohio, because she had two sisters living there. And she went to work in the bomber plant there in Cleveland. And so, I went to where she was, and she had a little apartment -- a second floor apartment, with -- she and my two younger sisters were living there. And I went there, and I slept in the living room on a couch for the next year and a half. I met -- I was going to college. I worked for the college. I went to work for the college before I started the college. I worked full-time for the college and I went to school full-time. And -- what do I call it -- I dated my wife, who became a wife, full-time. So I had three full-time jobs. Boy, it was terrible. And many a night, I was taking care of furnaces in a couple of places, and one of the girls -- homes where there was about a dozen girls living there -- and there was two coal-fired furnaces in the basement. And I had to dampen those off and everything. And I was out with my wife -- my girlfriend at that time -- came home and I got all ready for bed and everything. It was midnight. "Ah!" I didn't take care of the [chuckling] I got up and got dressed -- snow deep -- went about a block away, walked around there. Those kind of things. It was a lot of fun. My mother worked for the college. She worked -- she was working for a little jewelry shop there in town, but she then worked for the college. And I graduated there, and then my younger sister, when she graduated from high school there, she went to Baltimore also. She graduated there. My sisters were 11 and 13 years younger than me, and they're both dead. One of them ten years ago. It doesn't make any sense to me, because here I'm 84 years old today. And one's been gone for ten years and the other for two years. And one was 11 years younger than me and one was 13 years younger than me. So I feel I've been a real fortunate individual. I've got a good wife. Married into a good family. We got along well with her in-laws. My mother lived with us in California for the last eight years of her life, because she was so crippled up with arthritis she couldn't move. Before she died, she says, "Arlen," -- that's my wife -- "takes better care of me than my daughters do." And I have nothing to complain about. And I wouldn't trade -- I wouldn't change any of it. I'm trying to be a good Christian, and I know where I'm going. And I'm -- in a way; I'm looking forward to it. You hate to leave -- you hate to leave your family and friends and all that kind of stuff in the beauty of this world that we live in, but I know there's another beautiful place. I've had -- I haven't told you in my personal experience, because that's a completely different story. And I had a heart attack, was in the hospital three separate times. And I had an out of body experience. And everything that has ever happened to me turned out for the good. Turned out for the good. For the best for me. I have had one other out of body experience that I have told nobody about except a couple -- except my wife -- she knows about it. And the three ministers that I have talked to. Altogether different than any other ones. And I have got an appointment -- I don't have the appointment -- but I can go any time with the local minister Bob Barber, and he knows all about. So, we're going to have a discussion again here in a couple of days. [chuckling]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You won't put that on tape though, right?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: No, people wouldn't believe it anyway. Well, the second one. The first one, you know certain -- the first body experience -- if you read about any of them at all, kind of similar to that, but the same. The second one was altogether different. And I -- I said -- I haven't told anybody yet. But I intend to tell now to my daughters. And I intend to tell it to one other person. Because I'm thoroughly, thoroughly convinced at this point in time. As I said, I'm pretty sure I know where I'm going. So, well, I could go into some more. I don't know how much more time we have.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I have more time, but it's up to you.

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: [chuckling] Well, you can't say much bad about the army to me -- I tell you -- even though I had some bad days in the army. We had some -- most of our officers in our company -- I said, we had 45 officers. And I didn't even know some of them. I got chewed out by one of them one day, because I told him to get busy and dig a ditch. [laughing] And it was one of our officers. He chewed me out. But, that was while we were in the Philippines. And we didn't have your insignias on at that time. And I -- we were separated so much at the time. We had air corps officers. We had air patrol officers. We had navy officers. We all looked alike to me. [chuckling] So, yeah. He was sitting -- first sergeant had got a hold of me and said, "Dig yourself a hole there. I want to get some water, so we can wash some clothes while we're here and everything." So two guys sitting on a log over there. One was cleaning his rifle. The other was just sitting watching him talking to him. So I said, I remember I says, "As soon as you clean your rifle, get over there and help that guy dig a hole there. And you can go over there right now since you're not doing anything." And he just looked at me. He said, "Don't you have enough of privates do that?" I said, "Privates? Hey, that's staff sergeant digging the ditch right now and I'm a master sergeant and I'm going to have to help." And so, I said, "Get over and do it." And he just kept looking at me and he said, "Don't you have enough enlisted men to do that?" And I said, "Enlisted men?" And then, he proceeded to chew me out. But, we got along all right. We had some mighty good officers. The officer that I had -- he was a year younger than me. I was at that time in Leyte I was 24, he was about 23. When he made first lieutenant -- he was a second lieutenant when he came into the company -- he made first lieutenant. He had me pin his bars on him, gave me his second lieutenant bar. And some of the other officers in the company took him out. They were still in the States at that time. They took him out that night and got him so drunk, he couldn't -- boy, he didn't know what he was doing. He was drinking what they call border makers or something I don't know where you drink it -- whiskey and then a beer chaser or something. I didn't drink. So I didn't know anything. But he -- next morning, boy, he was hung over. And he came -- he was on duty and all. And I said -- he found me and he says, "Hey, Gross, can you cover for me today?" He says, "I got to find a place to sleep this off." He said. So he and I got along real well. Yeah it was funny. But, oh, there was some funny things that happened. And there was serious things that happened. And yeah, one of our men committed suicide. He'd been wounded on Leyte, and he saved up all his pain pills. We didn't know it. All these pain pills. And he got to -- he came back to the company at Okinawa. He said, "I'm never going back to the front again. Never going back; no way." And he took all of his pills at one time. He went into a --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Coma?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: Coma. And they put him in that hospital that was full of Japanese prisoners. That's how I got into the hospital right next to him. We took him over there. He died about a day and a half later. But, I -- and again, I'm going to say, he committed suicide. But I think they reported him as killed in action, so that his family could -- he had been wounded in action really on Leyte and everything. I'm pretty sure. But then we lost -- all of our company -- on the landings at Lusan. We lost over company records. The company safe and everything was on one vehicle. Either they dropped the vehicle in the ocean or something, but it was gone. So we lost all of our records for everything. And so, they had to just make them up with what they could and everything. So they reported him killed in action I think. All kinds of good times, bad times. But, just to show you -- and, you know, we're both -- we're all was working for the U.S. and everything like that. But we were these few army men at camp or marine base. When we went into town, Oceanside was the closest town there. When we went into town there, we walked in the streets, not on the sidewalks. Because the sidewalks were full of marines. [chuckling] Good master sergeant, I didn't smoke and I didn't drink and I didn't swear. And some people said, "Well, how did you manage?" I said, "I got along. I didn't care whether they made fun of me and everything." And I knew what I was doing. I got along with the people all right. Never had any troubles. I had a friend that threatened to kill me one night. But when he sobered up and knew what he said [chuckling] Why.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why did he threaten you?

sp.speaker: Harold Paul Gross
sp.p: I turned his bunk over. I was in charge that morning, and we were packing our stuff. This was at camp San Luis Obispo. There was two of us master sergeants, and the other one had gotten married, and he was living off base. And he asked me to take the morning, and I said, "Yeah, no problem." So we were packing stuff, and I had a whole crew down there. And we went down -- and this one buck sergeant -- Skelter by name -- he lives in southern Illinois -- and he still lives there. Good friend of mine. He'd been out the night before and gotten drunk. And he was sleeping it off up there. And he didn't get up. We didn't actually have a reveille because of the way we were situated. I called morning roll and he wasn't there. And he started working. And a guy said, "Where's Skelter? Where's Skelter?" And they kept looking at me. And I said, "Well, I'll go see." So I went up in the barracks. And I knew he was up there. And he was sleeping it off. And I tried to get him awake. And I yelled at him and pushed him and shoved him and everything. And finally, I turned his bunk over. [chuckling] He came up swinging. He come up swinging, "I'll kill you SOB!" So I took off. I wasn't about to have a fight with him, because he was bigger and stronger than me anyway. So I went back down to where the guys were working there. They looked at me and I didn't pay any attention. And about five minutes later, here comes Skelter. He comes down, and he sort of sidled over to me, and he says, "Hey, Gross, you didn't turn me in did you?" I said, "No Skelch, I've known you for a couple years. I've known you since I've been in the army. I know what your problem was." And I says, "Why should I make an enemy out of somebody when I can be friends with you?" And I says -- he was a buck sergeant; I was a master sergeant -- and I says, "I'm not going to have you busted." I could have had him busted just like that, because we had other guys busted by master sergeants like me. I said, "No, getting you busted ain't going to gain me anything." But I said, "Just be a little bit more careful when you threaten somebody like that." So we always got along after that. We've been good friends ever since. That was sort of my outlook on life. And I enjoyed the five years in the army overall. It turned out good for me.
